meta.title: Who really said "When they call the roll in the Senate... 'Present' or 'Not Guilty'"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Roosevelt. Wikiquote files it as Disputed with no citation at all. The joke is in print from March 1904 about the New York legislature, and was credited from 1905 to Rep. J. Adam Bede.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said ‘When they call the roll in the Senate, the Senators do not know whether to answer “Present” or “Not Guilty”’?
meta.ogDescription: No period source ties it to Theodore Roosevelt. It surfaces in March 1904 as an anonymous jab at the New York legislature, and by 1905 was Rep. J. Adam Bede's stock line about the Senate.

answer.label: Not Theodore Roosevelt — a 1904 newspaper joke
answer.authorDates: 1856–1942 · U.S. Representative from Minnesota · the House’s resident humorist
answer.sourceLine: Roosevelt has no documented connection to this line — Wikiquote lists it among his disputed quotations with no source attached at all, and in over a century of repetition nobody has produced one. The joke was already in American newspapers by March 1904, aimed at the New York legislature rather than the Senate and credited to nobody in particular. Within a year it had found its most famous mouth: from February 1905 the papers attribute it to J. Adam Bede, the Minnesota congressman whose stock-in-trade was exactly this kind of line. Bede almost certainly did not invent it either — he was, on the evidence, its best salesman.

source.heading: Where the joke actually comes from

docMeta.dd: the New York legislature at Albany — not the U.S. Senate

source.excerpt: This assemblyman of whom Mr. Shober tells is reported to have said that when the roll was called in the New York legislature, half the members did not know whether they were expected to answer ‘present’ or ‘not guilty.’
trail: Start with the credit itself, because it collapses immediately. Wikiquote carries the line on Roosevelt’s page under Disputed — and unlike every other entry in that section, it is a bare bullet with no citation whatsoever: no book, no speech, no date, not even a bad secondary source to argue with Wikiquote, Theodore Roosevelt (Disputed) ↗.

So we went to the newspapers instead. Searching the Library of Congress’s Chronicling America corpus for the exact phrasing, the earliest printing we located is the Portland Daily Press of 24 March 1904 — and it is not about the Senate at all. It reports an unnamed New York City assemblyman joking that at roll call in the New York legislature, half the members did not know whether to answer ‘present’ or ‘not guilty’ Portland Daily Press, 24 Mar 1904 ↗. A week later a Nevada paper ran the same gag about its own statehouse Morning Appeal, 31 Mar 1904 ↗, and by September it had been promoted to the U.S. Senate, still with nobody’s name on it Minneapolis Journal, 2 Sep 1904 ↗.

The name that period sources do attach is not Roosevelt’s. In February 1905 the Wausau Pilot reports that ‘Adam Bede, the acknowledged wit of the House, said the other day that things had come to such a pass in the United States Senate that on roll call the Senators were uncertain whether to answer present or not guilty’ Wausau Pilot, 14 Feb 1905 ↗. That November an Iowa paper credits the same man again, ‘Adam Bede, the humorist congressman of Minnesota’ Denison Review, 29 Nov 1905 ↗.

And the credit stuck with him, not with the President. In January 1910 the New-York Tribune quotes a sitting senator describing his first roll call: ‘I heard my name called, and I knew it was my name, but in the language of Adam Bede, I didn’t know whether to answer “present” or “not guilty”’ New-York Tribune, 21 Jan 1910 ↗. Five years on, in the Senate itself, the joke was Bede’s — and Roosevelt, then the most quoted man in America, was nowhere near it.

author.name: J. Adam Bede
author.heading: About J. Adam Bede
author.metaLine: 1856–1942 · U.S. Representative from Minnesota, 1903–1909 · newspaperman and humorist
author.bio: James Adam Bede was an Ohio-born newspaper editor who settled in Pine City, Minnesota, and went to Washington as a Republican congressman for three terms, 1903 to 1909. He was known less for legislation than for being the funniest man in the House — a stump speaker of, as the New York Times put it, ‘dry humor’ and ‘droll manner’. That reputation is why the papers of 1905 attached this joke to him by name, and why a senator was still quoting ‘the language of Adam Bede’ five years later.

misattribution.heading: How Roosevelt got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is a clean example of a quotation drifting upward. A joke told by a mid-ranking congressman about his colleagues is a footnote; the same joke in the mouth of Theodore Roosevelt is a quotation. Somewhere in the twentieth century the line made that jump, and nobody wrote down when.

items.why: Wikiquote files it under Roosevelt’s Disputed heading as a bare bullet with no citation at all — no work, no speech, no date. Every other entry in that section at least names a book to be sceptical about. This one names nothing Wikiquote, Theodore Roosevelt ↗.

items.who: An unnamed New York assemblyman, March 1904
items.why: The earliest printing we located is the Portland Daily Press of 24 March 1904, reporting the crack second-hand about the New York legislature. No author is named, and the U.S. Senate does not enter into it the 1904 printing ↗.

From February 1905 the papers put the Senate version in Bede’s mouth by name, and were still doing so in 1910, when a senator quoted it as ‘the language of Adam Bede’ New-York Tribune, 1910 ↗. Bede was a professional funny man — a newspaperman turned congressman, remembered for exactly this register J. Adam Bede ↗.

items.tag: the same joke, a new owner
items.why: Twenty years on, an Alabama paper reports Senator Copeland telling a bottlers’ convention ‘that when they call the roll in congress, the members don’t know whether to answer “present” or “not guilty”’. A joke this portable acquires a new author roughly every decade, which is how it eventually reached a President Birmingham Age-Herald, 24 Nov 1924 ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Roosevelt is the one name the period record never offers. The line is a newspaper joke about a state legislature from March 1904, and the man his own contemporaries credited for the Senate version was Rep. J. Adam Bede of Minnesota Wausau Pilot, 14 Feb 1905 ↗.

context.heading: Why it sounds like Roosevelt
lead: The joke belongs to a very specific moment. In the middle of the decade a run of United States senators were genuinely under indictment or serving sentences, and the papers of the day worked that fact hard. The Iowa paper that printed the gag in November 1905 sets it directly beside a note that ‘Senator Mitchell is serving time for his delinquencies’ and a tally of ‘the entire body of convicted senators at this time’. The line was not a general sneer at politicians; it was a topical crack about men who were, at that moment, actually facing juries.

Which is also why it reads as Rooseveltian. Roosevelt was the era’s loudest scourge of corrupt wealth and crooked politics, and he had the verbal manner to match — punchy, contemptuous, quotable. An unattributed joke about crooked senators drifts naturally toward the most quotable anti-corruption voice of the decade. It is the same mechanism that hands Churchill every good wartime line and Twain every good one-liner: the quote goes to whoever it sounds most like, not to whoever said it.
detailsBody: James Adam Bede (1856–1942) was a Minnesota newspaperman who went to Congress as a Republican, serving three terms from March 1903 to March 1909 — precisely the years this joke was circulating with his name on it.

He was famous in Washington for being funny, which in 1905 was a distinct political speciality. The New York Times, writing on humour in Congress in 1912, called him ‘one of the most popular stump speakers and spellbinders of the present generation’, whose speeches were ‘full of dry humor’.
Sharing a name with the title character of George Eliot’s 1859 novel did him no harm on the stump, and is one reason he is easy to lose in a search today.
He lost his renomination in 1908, went back to Pine City to publish and lecture, later served a term in the Minnesota House, and died in Duluth in 1942.
context.pull: A joke this portable acquires a new author about every decade. Roosevelt was simply the biggest name it ever reached.

schema.verdictNote: Commonly misattributed to Theodore Roosevelt, for whom no source has ever been produced. The joke appears in print from March 1904, initially unattributed and about the New York legislature; from February 1905 contemporaries credited Rep. J. Adam Bede, who popularised the Senate version but probably did not originate it.
